content: 1. In 2005, a Community Transport Plan (CTP) was developed in Nepal to facilitate the emergency transfer of women seeking obstetric care from villages to the nearest maternity unit. This quasi-experimental study was conducted in both urban and rural sites, with youth-centered participation. A comprehensive needs assessment was performed using triangulated methodologies, followed by community action planning to design the program. At control sites, a limited needs assessment was conducted, and three interventions based on current reproductive health knowledge and standard practices were implemented. In contrast, study sites identified eight integrated interventions addressing sexual and reproductive health needs of young people and broader social needs. 2. In 2010, the Familias Sanas intervention in Phoenix, Arizona, USA, aimed to bridge the cultural gap between Latina women and the healthcare system. Bilingual, bicultural Prenatal Partners acted as cultural brokers, providing ongoing antenatal care education and support services. This intervention adapted maternity care services to align with cultural needs and followed WHO recommendations on health promotion interventions for maternal and newborn health. 3. In 1990, the Asian Mother and Baby Campaign in Leicestershire, England, targeted Asian women to address their specific maternal health needs. 4. In 2006, in the rural Siraha district of Nepal, community health workers (CHWs) used a birth preparedness (BP) package with flip charts and distributed keychains containing BP messages. These were shared during monthly discussions in women’s groups. 5. In 2010, a cluster randomized controlled trial in rural Khuzdar district, Balochistan, Pakistan, provided women and their husbands with pictorial booklets and audio cassettes. Birth attendants were trained to recognize obstetric danger signs early, and transportation and telecommunication services were established for emergency obstetric and neonatal care. The intervention included women-only and couples’ groups, training of traditional birth attendants (TBAs) for clean home delivery, and training of local vehicle owners for referral services. Healthcare providers in both intervention and control arms received clinical training. 6. In 1991, a hospital-based cohort study in rural Kilifi district, Zimbabwe, established a maternity waiting home (MWH) within a two-minute walk from the maternity ward. 7. In 2006, in Koupela, Burkina Faso, community and facility-based healthcare workers (HCWs) and skilled birth attendants (SBAs) provided one-on-one counseling to pregnant women and families on birth preparedness and complication readiness (BPCR) using flip charts. These messages were reinforced through district-based radio messages and theater plays. 8. In 2007, a randomized controlled trial in Kathmandu, Nepal, involved couples and women who received two health education sessions from health educators. The control group received no education, only a brief flyer resembling standard health education. 9. In 2010, a preand post-intervention study in Myanmar (Shan, Mon, Karen, and Karenni regions) implemented a community-based project to improve maternal health service coverage in vulnerable communities. 10. In 2010, in rural Mtwara region, Tanzania, safe motherhood promoters were trained to educate and raise awareness about maternal health among pregnant women, husbands, and community members through home visits. 11. In 2003, a descriptive study in remote northern and western Queensland, Australia, involved consultations with health providers and Aboriginal communities. The program included an Indigenous medical center managed by a community board, staffed by Indigenous people, home visits, transportation provision, and family involvement in ongoing care. 12. In 2005, a prospective cohort study in Townsville, North Queensland, Australia, collaborated with Indigenous communities to develop an integrated model of antenatal shared care delivered through the community-controlled Townsville Aboriginal and Islander Health Service. 13. In 1992, a retrospective study in Hackney, East London, UK, introduced the Multi-Ethnic Women’s Health Project, a health advocacy program at a hospital to meet the needs of non-English-speaking women. 14. In 2005, a one-group preand post-evaluation study in India implemented a local initiatives program. 15. In 1990, a hospital-based cohort study in rural Ethiopia established a maternity waiting home (MWH) with 15 beds near a hospital delivery unit. The MWH was built in the style of a local house, and women were accompanied by a relative, supplied their own food, and purchased firewood locally. 16. In 2009, a program evaluation in Hangu district, Pakistan, involved male involvement interventions for safe motherhood. Services were established, and training was provided to community actors, including TBAs, to raise awareness of services and reproductive health issues. Each refugee camp had a health committee with community representatives and health service staff who met bi-monthly to discuss project activities and provide feedback. Basic emergency obstetric care facilities and community-based education were provided to key community representatives. 17. In 2001, a preand post-intervention study in South Kalimantan, Indonesia, placed a midwife in each village and at least one doctor with obstetric skills in each district. Financial access was facilitated for the poor, and village midwives were encouraged to work alongside TBAs. 18. In 2008, a one-group preand post-evaluation study in rural Andhra Pradesh, India, involved village meetings and community activities to increase demand for quality pregnancy-related services. The intervention included awareness-raising and community support for pregnant women through local government and youth committees, family involvement (especially husbands) in pregnancy-related care, and bi-monthly home visits by a community organizer to create birth preparedness plans. 19. In 2004, a preand post-comparative study in West Java, Indonesia, implemented social mobilization campaigns. The Suami SIAGA (alert husband) campaign encouraged community members to prepare for births, and the Bidan SIAGA campaign promoted midwives as preferred maternal healthcare providers. 20. In 2004, a one-group preand post-evaluation study in rural districts of Baglung and Lalitpur, Nepal, implemented the SUMATA campaign, a multimedia behavioral change strategy targeting husbands and mothers-in-law. 21. In 1998, a community-based cohort study in Mberengwa district, Zimbabwe, established maternity waiting homes (MWHs) on the premises of four of the five hospitals in the district, covering 22 clinics offering maternity services. 22. In 1996, a hospital-based cohort study in rural Chimanimani district, Zimbabwe, established a simple maternity waiting home (MWH) close to the hospital. Women stayed during the last month of gestation and were transferred to the hospital if complications developed or labor began. 23. In 2011, a quasi-experimental preand post-study in Eritrea trained community members (women and men) to become maternal health volunteers and lead participatory education sessions. Skills training for healthcare providers was also conducted. 24. In 2008, a case study in rural India used a detailed verbal autopsy questionnaire to identify missing links in officially recorded data, reconstruct the sequence of events, and pinpoint the exact cause of maternal deaths. 25. In 1999, a household-level cross-sectional survey in rural Gutu district, Zimbabwe, did not describe any specific intervention. 26. In 2003, a hospital-based cohort study in rural Eastern Province, Zambia, established a maternity waiting home (MWH) next to the maternity ward. Women with high-risk pregnancies were referred during the last weeks of pregnancy. The hospital provided food for women at the MWH and charged a reduced fee for those who stayed in the MWH. 27. In 2012, a hospital-based before-and-after study in Timor-Leste established small maternity waiting homes (MWHs) next to facilities. All women stayed together in a large room with food provided, and childbirth facilities were moved to the MWH.
